name: Applied Cryptography
description: Practical cryptographic constructions, attacks on deployed crypto, and crypto engineering.

uss.narrative:
The earliest papers on this list, from USENIX 2018, set a tone that runs through the whole period: applied cryptography is less about inventing new schemes and more about finding where deployed crypto breaks. Several 2018 works attacked the machinery the internet already relies on. "Bamboozling Certificate Authorities with BGP" (USENIX 2018) showed that the web PKI's domain-validation process could be subverted by hijacking routes, while "Return Of Bleichenbacher's Oracle Threat (ROBOT)" (USENIX 2018) demonstrated that a twenty-year-old RSA padding-oracle attack was still alive across major TLS stacks. Alongside protocol attacks, this year emphasized implementation leakage: "DATA - Differential Address Trace Analysis" (USENIX 2018) and "One&Done: A Single-Decryption EM-Based Attack on OpenSSL's Constant-Time Blinded RSA" (USENIX 2018) showed that even constant-time code leaks through address traces and electromagnetic emanations, and "Efail" (USENIX 2018) exposed how email encryption standards leak plaintext through exfiltration channels.

Over 2019 and 2020 the field broadened from breaking things to measuring and protecting real systems at scale. "Protecting accounts from credential stuffing with password breach alerting" (USENIX 2019) and "in-toto" (USENIX 2019) reframed crypto as infrastructure for everyday account and software-supply-chain security, and "The KNOB is Broken" (USENIX 2019) extended the attack tradition into Bluetooth key negotiation. By 2020 two threads matured in parallel: attacks kept landing on widely deployed crypto, with "SHA-1 is a Shambles" (USENIX 2020) producing the first chosen-prefix collision on SHA-1 and "Call Me Maybe: ReVoLTE" (USENIX 2020) eavesdropping on encrypted LTE calls, while constructive work like "Pancake: Frequency Smoothing for Encrypted Data Stores" (USENIX 2020) and "Big Numbers - Big Troubles" (USENIX 2020) tackled access-pattern leakage and systematic nonce leakage in (EC)DSA.

From 2021 onward the center of gravity shifted toward two newer engines: zero-knowledge proofs and privacy-preserving computation over real data. "Poseidon: A New Hash Function for Zero-Knowledge Proof Systems" (USENIX 2021), by far the most cited paper on this list, signaled how central SNARK/STARK-friendly primitives had become, a line continued by "Eos: Efficient Private Delegation of zkSNARK Provers" (USENIX 2023). At the same time, private set intersection and private information retrieval moved from theory to deployable tools in "Fuzzy Labeled Private Set Intersection" (USENIX 2021), "Constant-weight PIR" (USENIX 2022), and "Efficient Unbalanced Private Set Intersection Cardinality" (USENIX 2023). Meanwhile the side-channel and protocol-audit traditions never went away but climbed the hardware stack and into shipped products, with "CIPHERLEAKS" (USENIX 2021) attacking AMD SEV's ciphertext channel, "Three Lessons From Threema" (USENIX 2023) cryptanalyzing a popular messenger, and "GoFetch" (USENIX 2024) defeating constant-time implementations through data-memory-dependent prefetchers. The throughline is clear: the area now spans rigorous cryptanalysis of deployed systems on one side and engineering practical advanced primitives like ZK proofs and PSI/PIR on the other.

ndss.narrative:
The earliest papers in this NDSS collection show applied cryptography working on two fronts at once: hardening systems people already deploy, and building trusted-hardware primitives. On the deployment side, "A Security Analysis of Honeywords" (NDSS 2018) probed decoy-password schemes, "Mind Your Keys? A Security Evaluation of Java Keystores" (NDSS 2018) found real flaws in how a widely used library stores keys, and "Cloud Strife: Mitigating the Security Risks of Domain-Validated Certificates" (NDSS 2018) exposed how cloud IP reuse undermines certificate issuance. In parallel, "ZeroTrace: Oblivious Memory Primitives from Intel SGX" (NDSS 2018) fused cryptography with SGX enclaves to hide memory access patterns, kicking off a hardware-plus-crypto thread that "OBFUSCURO: A Commodity Obfuscation Engine on Intel SGX" (NDSS 2019) and "Giving State to the Stateless" (NDSS 2019) would extend.

Around 2019, blockchain became the field's center of gravity. "Anonymous Multi-Hop Locks for Blockchain Scalability and Interoperability" (NDSS 2019) gave payment channels a cryptographic backbone, "Fine-Grained and Controlled Rewriting in Blockchains" (NDSS 2019) reworked chameleon hashes for redactable ledgers, and "Vault: Fast Bootstrapping for the Algorand Cryptocurrency" (NDSS 2019) attacked the practical problem of joining a chain cheaply. Alongside this, careful analysis of deployed crypto matured: "Analyzing Semantic Correctness with Symbolic Execution: A Case Study on PKCS#1 v1.5 Signature Verification" (NDSS 2019) used symbolic execution to catch signature-verification bugs, and later "Shadow Attacks: Hiding and Replacing Content in Signed PDFs" (NDSS 2021) showed signed documents could still be silently altered.

The 2020-2023 stretch is dominated by encrypted search and oblivious access. Private information retrieval and searchable encryption became a running theme, from "Heterogeneous Private Information Retrieval" (NDSS 2020) and "Practical Non-Interactive Searchable Encryption with Forward and Backward Privacy" (NDSS 2021) through "Obfuscated Access and Search Patterns in Searchable Encryption" (NDSS 2021) and "OBI: a multi-path oblivious RAM for forward-and-backward-secure searchable encryption" (NDSS 2023), which tied ORAM techniques back to searchable encryption. Threshold cryptography also came of age with "Real Threshold ECDSA" (NDSS 2023), reflecting demand from custody and DNSSEC deployments, while randomness beacons like "OptRand" (NDSS 2023) addressed the decentralized-trust plumbing these systems need.

The most recent work points squarely at two frontiers: post-quantum migration and homomorphic/multi-party computation at scale. "When Cryptography Needs a Hand: Practical Post-Quantum Authentication for V2V Communications" (NDSS 2024) and "Looma: A Low-Latency PQTLS Authentication Architecture for Cloud Applications" (NDSS 2026) tackle the overhead of moving TLS and vehicular authentication to PQC, while "HEIR: A Unified Representation for Cross-Scheme Compilation of Fully Homomorphic Computation" (NDSS 2024) and "Select-Then-Compute: Encrypted Label Selection and Analytics over Distributed Datasets using FHE" (NDSS 2026) push FHE toward practical analytics. The 2026 slate is otherwise a maturing mix: faster private set intersection and union ("Faster Than Ever: A New Lightweight Private Set Intersection and Its Variants", "cwPSU"), systematization such as "SoK: Cryptographic Authenticated Dictionaries", private auctions in "Cryptobazaar", and a reminder that attacks keep pace with constructions in "Learning from Leakage: Database Reconstruction from Just a Few Multidimensional Range Queries" (NDSS 2026).

sp.narrative:
The earliest listed work, clustered at IEEE S&P 2018, already staked out the two poles that still organize applied cryptography: building better primitives and breaking deployed ones. On the constructive side, "Bulletproofs: Short Proofs for Confidential Transactions and More" (S&P 2018) delivered compact zero-knowledge range proofs with no trusted setup, while "Doubly-Efficient zkSNARKs Without Trusted Setup" (S&P 2018) and "Secure Two-party Threshold ECDSA from ECDSA Assumptions" (S&P 2018) answered the cryptocurrency-driven demand for succinct proofs and split-key signing. On the attack side, "Improved Reconstruction Attacks on Encrypted Data Using Range Query Leakage" (S&P 2018) showed that searchable/encrypted databases leak enough through access patterns to reconstruct plaintext — a theme that matured into "Learning to Reconstruct" (S&P 2019) and "The State of the Uniform" (S&P 2020), which stripped away the convenient uniform-query assumption.

Two big shifts followed. First, zero-knowledge went from a specialized tool to core infrastructure: "Transparent Polynomial Delegation" (S&P 2020) and "Wolverine" (S&P 2021) drove down setup requirements and communication cost, and systems like "ZEXE" (S&P 2020) and "FlyClient" (S&P 2020) folded proofs into real ledgers and light clients. Second, threshold and distributed cryptography scaled from two parties to committees — "Threshold ECDSA from ECDSA Assumptions: The Multiparty Case" (S&P 2019), "Towards Scalable Threshold Cryptosystems" (S&P 2020), and "Practical Asynchronous Distributed Key Generation" (S&P 2022) — reflecting a move from single-signer security to fault-tolerant, trust-distributed deployment.

Running alongside was a quiet but decisive turn toward assurance and usable advanced encryption. "Simple High-Level Code for Cryptographic Arithmetic" (S&P 2019) and "EverCrypt" (S&P 2020) proved that formally verified implementations could be as fast as hand-tuned ones, a program the community consolidated in "SoK: Computer-Aided Cryptography" (S&P 2021). In parallel, homomorphic encryption edged toward practicality with "PEGASUS" (S&P 2021) and the tooling survey "SoK: Fully Homomorphic Encryption Compilers" (S&P 2021), joined by private-database systems such as "Waldo" (S&P 2022) and secure aggregation for federated learning in "Flamingo" (S&P 2023).

The most recent work at S&P 2026 shows the field simultaneously generalizing its proof machinery and confronting the post-quantum horizon and messy real deployments. Proof systems now target whole machine executions and structured data rather than fixed circuits, as in "Nebula: Proving Machine Executions via Folding Schemes" and "Coral: Fast Succinct Non-Interactive Zero-Knowledge CFG Proofs," alongside efforts to outsource proving in "Single-Server Private Outsourcing of zk-SNARKs." Post-quantum concerns move to the foreground with "A Maliciously-Secure Post-Quantum OPRF from Crypto Dark Matter" and "Blinding Post-Quantum Hash-and-Sign Signatures," while FHE-backed databases resurface in "APEX." At the same time, the attack tradition endures against fielded systems, with "STIR/SHAKEN: A Cocktail of Cryptographic Clumsiness" and "Secret State Leakage Attacks and Their Impacts on EMV Contactless Payment Apps" dissecting cryptography as actually deployed — a fitting bookend to the leakage attacks that opened this window.

ccs.narrative:
Applied cryptography at ACM CCS has consistently sat at the intersection of theory and practice, with CCS serving as the premier venue for work that deploys cryptographic ideas in real systems. Early in the dataset (2018-2019), the community was heavily focused on searchable encryption and encrypted databases, producing foundational works such as New Constructions for Forward and Backward Private Symmetric Searchable Encryption (CCS 2018) and Pump up the Volume: Practical Database Reconstruction from Volume Leakage on Range Queries (CCS 2018), which together framed the tension between efficiency and leakage. Threshold ECDSA and distributed key management emerged as another major thread, with Fast Multiparty Threshold ECDSA with Fast Trustless Setup (CCS 2018) and Fast Secure Multiparty ECDSA with Practical Distributed Key Generation and Applications to Cryptocurrency Custody (CCS 2018) driving cryptocurrency custody applications.

The 2019-2020 period saw growing attention to cryptographic infrastructure at internet scale. Let's Encrypt: An Automated Certificate Authority to Encrypt the Entire Web (CCS 2019) documented the CA system that flipped the web to HTTPS, while CryptoGuard: High Precision Detection of Cryptographic Vulnerabilities in Massive-sized Java Projects (CCS 2019) attacked the problem of misuse of cryptographic APIs in practice. Zero-knowledge proof systems matured dramatically, with Ligero++: A New Optimized Sublinear IOP (CCS 2020) pushing toward transparency and avoiding trusted setups.

From 2022 onward, ZK proofs crossed into production blockchains and AI. zkBridge: Trustless Cross-chain Bridges Made Practical (CCS 2022) demonstrated verifiable cross-chain state transfer, while zkLLM: Zero Knowledge Proofs for Large Language Models (CCS 2024) extended the paradigm to certifying LLM inference. Attribute-based encryption, post-quantum constructions, and FHE-friendly primitives such as Chaghri - A FHE-friendly Block Cipher (CCS 2022) and FABEO: Fast Attribute-Based Encryption with Optimal Security (CCS 2022) continued to push the efficiency frontier.

milestones.title: New Constructions for Forward and Backward Private Symmetric Searchable Encryption

top4.narrative:
The earliest work in this slice, all from 2018, shows applied cryptography splitting along a few durable lines. On the constructive side, zero-knowledge proofs matured from theory into deployable tools: "Bulletproofs: Short Proofs for Confidential Transactions and More" (S&P 2018) delivered short, trustless range proofs that cryptocurrencies adopted almost immediately, while "Doubly-Efficient zkSNARKs Without Trusted Setup" (S&P 2018) attacked the trusted-setup problem that had dogged succinct proofs. In parallel, a wave of threshold-signature papers — "Secure Two-party Threshold ECDSA from ECDSA Assumptions" (S&P 2018) alongside CCS 2018's "Fast Multiparty Threshold ECDSA" and "Fast Secure Multiparty ECDSA with Practical Distributed Key Generation" — made it practical to split a signing key across parties, driven by cryptocurrency custody needs.

The other half of 2018 was destructive, and just as important. "Return Of Bleichenbacher's Oracle Threat (ROBOT)" (USENIX 2018) showed a two-decade-old RSA padding attack still breaking real TLS stacks, and "One&Done" (USENIX 2018) pulled an RSA key from a single EM trace, underscoring how gaps between clean math and messy implementations keep biting deployed systems. A second attack thread targeted encrypted databases: "Improved Reconstruction Attacks on Encrypted Data Using Range Query Leakage" (S&P 2018) and "Pump up the Volume" (CCS 2018) showed that even without breaking the cipher, query and volume leakage can reconstruct plaintext — a direct rebuttal to the searchable-encryption schemes appearing the same year, like CCS 2018's forward/backward-private constructions.

The 2019-2022 span shows these threads consolidating and scaling. Threshold ECDSA generalized to the full multiparty case ("Threshold ECDSA from ECDSA Assumptions: The Multiparty Case," S&P 2019) and gained robustness features ("UC Non-Interactive, Proactive, Threshold ECDSA with Identifiable Aborts," CCS 2020). Zero-knowledge kept accelerating: "Poseidon: A New Hash Function for Zero-Knowledge Proof Systems" (USENIX 2021) built a hash tuned for arithmetic circuits, "Wolverine" (S&P 2021) pushed communication-efficient proofs, and "zkBridge: Trustless Cross-chain Bridges Made Practical" (CCS 2022) applied proofs to connect blockchains. The field also began auditing itself, with "SoK: Computer-Aided Cryptography" (S&P 2021) and the misuse-detector "CryptoGuard" (CCS 2019) turning attention to whether the crypto is implemented correctly at all.

The most recent work, clustered in NDSS 2026, shows the area both broadening and bracing for the post-quantum transition. "Looma: A Low-Latency PQTLS Authentication Architecture for Cloud Applications" confronts quantum threats to TLS directly, while private-computation primitives keep getting lighter and more specialized — "Faster Than Ever: A New Lightweight Private Set Intersection," "cwPSU: Efficient Unbalanced Private Set Union," and FHE-based analytics in "Select-Then-Compute." Notably, the 2018 attack line is still alive: "Learning from Leakage: Database Reconstruction from Just a Few Multidimensional Range Queries" (NDSS 2026) extends the range-query reconstruction attacks to multidimensional data, a direct descendant of the 2018 leakage papers. Systematization is now a fixture too ("SoK: Cryptographic Authenticated Dictionaries," NDSS 2026), signaling a field that has enough mature building blocks to start organizing them.
